topic: Why the Sunny 16 rule works: f/16 at 1/ISO (1/125 s at ISO 100) = EV log2(16^2 x 125) = log2(32000) ~ 15.0 = standard EV100 for a typical scene in full sun (~82,000 lux by the standard calibration); each stop wider halves the time and keeps the same exposure
lines: On a sunny day, you don't need a light meter.
Set your aperture to f sixteen, and your shutter speed to one over your ISO. At ISO one hundred, that's a hundred and twenty-fifth of a second.
Set your aperture to f/16, and your shutter speed to 1 over your ISO. At ISO 100, that's 1/125 of a second.
Why? Exposure depends on the aperture squared, divided by the shutter time. Call it exposure value, E V.
Why? Exposure depends on the aperture squared, divided by the shutter time. Call it exposure value, EV.
Sixteen squared is two fifty-six. Divide by one over a hundred twenty-five: thirty-two thousand. Take the base two logarithm: fifteen.
16 squared is 256. Divide by 1 over 125: 32,000. Take the base 2 logarithm: 15.
E V fifteen is the standard value for a typical scene in full sun at ISO one hundred. More than eighty thousand lux.
EV 15 is the standard value for a typical scene in full sun at ISO 100. More than 80,000 lux.
Open one stop, to f eleven, and you need half the time. Same exposure. Same at f eight, and f five point six.
Open one stop, to f/11, and you need half the time. Same exposure. Same at f/8, and f/5.6.
The sun doesn't change. So neither do your settings.

youtube.title: Why "Sunny 16" Works: The Math Behind f/16 and 1/ISO
youtube.description:
The Sunny 16 rule: in direct sun, set the aperture to f/16 and the shutter speed to 1/ISO (about 1/125 s at ISO 100). It works because exposure value is EV = log2(N²/t): f/16 at 1/125 s gives log2(256 × 125) = log2(32,000) ≈ 15.0, which is the standard EV100 for a typical scene in full sun. By the standard meter calibration that is roughly 82,000 lux. Open the aperture one stop (f/11) and halve the exposure time (1/250 s) and the exposure stays the same. The frames are a simulation (illustrative blur scales), not photos.

sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_16_rule (f/16 and shutter = 1/ISO; ISO 100 -> 1/100 or 1/125 s; exposure ~ 1/N^2 x t, one stop = factor ~sqrt2, e.g. 1/250 s at f/11 = 1/125 s at f/16)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exposure_value (EV = log2(N^2/t); EV100 = 15 for a typical scene in full or slightly hazy sunlight with distinct shadows; with C = 250 lux*s*ISO, EV 15 'sunny sixteen' = 82,000 lux)
Check: log2(16^2 x 125) = log2(32000) = 14.97; f/11 1/250 = 14.88; f/8 1/500 = 14.97; f/5.6 1/1000 = 14.94. Frames are a numpy simulation with illustrative blur scales.
